Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Public Transport: Bus riding, Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Priya

Priya was twenty-two when the police stopped the bus she was riding home from her community center in Jersey City, where she had spent the evening volunteering as a peer counselor. The stop came without warning—lights, sirens, officers boarding with hands on their belts. What began as a routine document check became something else when one officer, seeing her name on her ID, demanded she step off the bus. She remembers the heat of the afternoon, the smell of diesel and the earth stirred up by the bus's brakes, the way his hand moved toward her when she hesitated. She remembers the concrete pressing into her ribs, his knee, the feeling that her body was no longer hers to control. The other passengers watched. No one intervened. Within minutes it was over, but the officer's face—the particular angle of his jaw, the coldness in his eyes—had burned itself into her nervous system.

Three years have passed, and Priya is now twenty-five. She still works as a counselor, but her world has contracted in ways that would be unrecognizable to the young woman she was before. The bus she once rode without thought has become impossible. She drives now, alone, her hands gripping the wheel, her eyes constantly checking the mirrors—not for traffic, but for police cars. The checking has become compulsive, a ritual she cannot stop even when she knows logically that no one is behind her. When she sees a patrol car at a distance, her body floods with adrenaline before her mind has even registered the threat; her hands shake, her breath shortens, and she has to pull over until the panic subsides.

The smell of soil or grass—scents that once meant her grandmother's garden, the earth where her family had roots—now trigger a cascade of sensory memories so vivid that Priya cannot distinguish between past and present. When she walks outside and catches the smell of damp earth, her body involuntarily tenses into the same rigid position it held on that concrete, and she feels the pressure of that officer's weight as though it were happening again, across every nerve. These moments come without warning, and they leave her shaken for hours.

Priya has stopped seeing friends from before the incident. She tells herself it is easier this way—that people cannot be trusted, that they will judge her or see her differently now. What frightens her most is that she has come to believe people are not what they seem, that beneath every friendly face there is potential danger. At work, she finds herself studying clients' expressions and body language obsessively, searching for signs of threat, reading hostility into neutral glances. This vigilance exhausts her. At night, she lies awake, unable to sleep, because her mind will not allow her body to rest. She needs to stay alert, to monitor, to be ready. She has convinced herself that sleep is a vulnerability she cannot afford.

She avoids looking at her own face. When she passes mirrors, she covers her face with her hands or looks away. She is not sure why, except that seeing her reflection feels like an accusation, as though her face is a reminder of what happened, evidence of contamination she cannot wash away no matter how many times she showers. The numbness that sometimes descends when she recalls the event is almost worse than the reliving—it feels like she is describing something that happened to someone else, and this disconnection terrifies her because it means she has lost even the right to her own experience.

Her supervisor recently asked if she was all right; Priya's work with clients has become more guarded, less warm. She said yes, but the question lodged in her. She came to therapy because she is afraid that the person she was—connected to her community, open to others, able to ride a bus without terror—is gone. What she hopes for most is not to forget, but to feel safe enough to live again.
